extracted.intended_audience: Appellants and practitioners involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings (persons seeking reconsideration under 37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c))
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for granting or denying a Request for Reconsideration of a USPTO Director's Final Order under 37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c), including what qualifies as 'new evidence' and what constitutes errors of law or fact sufficient to alter a final disciplinary decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible grounds for reconsideration under § 11.56(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may grant a request for reconsideration or modification of the Final Order if the request is based on newly discovered evidence, or an error of law or fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard of review for § 11.56(c) requests is narrow and limited; the courts' standards for motions under Fed. R. Civ. P. 59(e) and 60 are applied as useful guidance. Reconsideration is allowed only where new evidence exists or where there are errors of law or fact that warrant modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newly discovered evidence must not have been available before the Final Order
rubrics_metrics.description: Any new evidence submitted must not have been available prior to issuance of the Final Order; evidence available to a party before entry of judgment is not a basis for reconsideration as a matter of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents that were part of the administrative record or otherwise in the party's possession (e.g., emails, correspondence, briefs, hearing transcripts) cannot be treated as 'new.' Case law: Boryan v. United States, 884 F.2d 767, 771; Frederick S. Wyle P.C. v. Texaco, Inc., 764 F.2d 604, 609. The requester must show the evidence truly could not have been discovered earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests cannot be used to relitigate or merely disagree with the Final Order
rubrics_metrics.description: A request for reconsideration is not a vehicle to state a party's disagreement with a final judgment or to rehash arguments previously presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere disagreement or repeating arguments that were presented to the ALJ or Director does not justify reconsideration. Authorities: Hutchinson v. Staton, 994 F.2d 1076, 1081-82; Arthur v. King, 500 F.3d 1335, 1343. Examples of improper use include reasserting the same objections, chronology, opinions, or excuses that were considered and rejected previously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors of fact must be actual factual errors that warrant dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: Alleged factual errors must be genuine mistakes in the Final Order's factual findings, not a mix of chronology, opinion, or mis-statements of procedural history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requesters must identify specific factual errors showing the decisionmaker erred (e.g., overlooked or mischaracterized testimony or documentary evidence in a way that affects the outcome). The Director is not obligated to reference every piece of evidence in the Final Order; claiming 'concealment' when the testimony was considered is insufficient. Repeating prior factual arguments that were adjudicated does not meet the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors of law must present new legal authority or show a manifest error
rubrics_metrics.description: Alleged errors of law must be more than reassertions of previously raised legal arguments; they must present new case law, changes in the law, or demonstrate that the decision was outside the adversarial issues or based on a misunderstanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A requester cannot prevail by arguing the Director exceeded statutory authority unless new authorities or changes in law are cited. To succeed, show the decisionmaker 'patently misunderstood' a party, made a decision 'outside the adversarial issues presented,' or made an 'error not of reasoning but of apprehension.' See Above the Belt, Inc. v. Mel Bohannan Roofing, Inc., 99 F.R.D. 99, 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration is an extraordinary remedy and rarely granted
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconsideration motions are extraordinary remedies reserved for extraordinary circumstances and should be used sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts limit relief to narrow circumstances (e.g., extraordinary circumstances under Rule 60(b)(6)). Authorities: Dowell v. State Farm Fire & Cas. Auto. Ins. Co., 993 F.2d 46, 48; Projects Mgmt. Co. v. DynCorp Int'l, LLC, 17 F. Supp. 3d 539, 541. The USPTO applies this high standard, and requests that merely repeat prior arguments or evidence will be denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence in possession or discoverable by the party is not 'new'
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents or information that the appellant possessed during the proceeding (including correspondence with OED counsel) are not newly discovered and therefore do not justify reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence could have been discovered or produced during the administrative hearing or on appeal (e.g., emails, letters, exhibits the appellant had), it will not be considered new. Labeling such materials as 'evidence' of error without showing they were unavailable earlier is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural next steps and timing for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: If the request for reconsideration is denied, the appellant may seek judicial review on the record in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia under 35 U.S.C. § 32.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any petition for judicial review must be filed 'within thirty (30) days after the date of the order recording the Director's action.' See E.D. Va. Local Civil Rule 83.5.
